pharm: Long-acting first-generation sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells by closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels; also has a mild antidiuretic (ADH-potentiating) effect.

Take with breakfast; single daily dose
Avoid; insulin is preferred (risk of neonatal hypoglycemia)
Avoid in significant impairment - hypoglycemia risk
Avoid - disulfiram-like flushing reaction and hypoglycemia
Blood glucose, HbA1c, serum sodium (SIADH/hyponatremia), renal function
summary: Chlorpropamide is a long-acting, first-generation sulfonylurea used as an adjunct to diet to lower blood glucose in type 2 diabetes mellitus. Because of its very long duration of action and renal elimination, it carries a high risk of prolonged, severe hypoglycemia, especially in the elderly and in renal impairment. It also potentiates antidiuretic hormone, causing water retention, SIADH, and hyponatremia, and can produce a disulfiram-like (flushing) reaction with alcohol. Sulfonylureas carry a class warning of increased cardiovascular mortality (based on the UGDP study). It has largely been superseded by shorter-acting agents.
indications: Adjunct to diet and exercise to lower blood glucose in adults with type 2 (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus when diet alone is inadequate

dosage.d: 250 mg once daily with breakfast (start 100-125 mg in older or debilitated patients)
Usual 100-500 mg once daily, adjusted in 50-125 mg steps every 3-5 days
750 mg per day (doses above 500-750 mg rarely add benefit and increase risk)
Start 100-125 mg once daily; titrate cautiously
dosage.n: High hypoglycemia risk; avoid if possible

admin: Take as a single daily dose with breakfast to reduce gastrointestinal upset
Maintain a consistent meal pattern; do not skip meals
Initiate at low doses, especially in the elderly, and titrate slowly because of the long half-life
Avoid alcohol due to the risk of a disulfiram-like (flushing) reaction
Monitor blood glucose and serum sodium during therapy
moa: Chlorpropamide is a first-generation sulfonylurea that lowers blood glucose primarily by stimulating insulin release from functioning pancreatic beta cells. It binds the sulfonylurea receptor (SUR1) on the beta-cell membrane, closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels; the resulting membrane depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, raising intracellular calcium and triggering insulin secretion. With chronic use it may also enhance peripheral insulin sensitivity. Distinct among sulfonylureas, chlorpropamide also potentiates the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) on the renal collecting duct, producing an antidiuretic effect that can cause water retention and hyponatremia (SIADH-like).

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to chlorpropamide or sulfonylureas
Diabetic ketoacidosis (with or without coma) - treat with insulin
relative: Elderly or debilitated/malnourished patients (high hypoglycemia risk)
Conditions predisposing to hyponatremia or fluid retention (heart failure, SIADH risk)
Concurrent drugs that potentiate hypoglycemia or alter sodium
monitor: Signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia (which may be prolonged)

preg: Chlorpropamide is not recommended in pregnancy; insulin is the preferred agent for diabetes in pregnancy. Sulfonylureas given near term can cause prolonged severe neonatal hypoglycemia. Discontinue and switch to insulin before a planned pregnancy if possible.
lact: Chlorpropamide is excreted in human milk and may cause hypoglycemia in the breastfed infant; breastfeeding is generally not recommended during therapy. If antidiabetic therapy is needed, consider insulin and avoid chlorpropamide.
renal: Chlorpropamide and its active metabolites are eliminated renally; in renal impairment the drug accumulates and can cause severe, prolonged hypoglycemia. It is contraindicated/should be avoided in significant renal impairment, and dose caution is needed even with mild impairment.
hepatic: Chlorpropamide is partly metabolized in the liver; in significant hepatic impairment, the risk of hypoglycemia is increased and clearance may be reduced. Avoid in significant hepatic impairment.

major: Alcohol - disulfiram-like (flushing) reaction and increased/erratic hypoglycemia
Other hypoglycemic agents (insulin, other sulfonylureas) - additive hypoglycemia
Drugs that potentiate hypoglycemia (sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones, salicylates in large doses, NSAIDs, MAO inhibitors, fibrates, beta-blockers which also mask symptoms) - increased hypoglycemia risk
moderate: Drugs that raise blood glucose / reduce control (thiazide and other diuretics, corticosteroids, estrogens/oral contraceptives, phenytoin, sympathomimetics, thyroid hormones, isoniazid) - may require dose adjustment
Coumarin anticoagulants - bidirectional changes in anticoagulant and chlorpropamide effects
Drugs/conditions causing hyponatremia (thiazides, carbamazepine) - additive hyponatremia/SIADH
minor: Beta-blockers may blunt the warning signs (tachycardia, tremor) of hypoglycemia
interactions.food: Take with breakfast; consistent carbohydrate intake helps avoid hypoglycemia. Missing meals increases hypoglycemia risk.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - chlorpropamide can cause a disulfiram-like flushing reaction (facial flushing, headache, nausea) and unpredictable hypoglycemia.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause hyponatremia (SIADH), abnormal liver tests, and rarely hematologic abnormalities; may produce a positive direct Coombs/hemolysis.

serious: Severe and prolonged hypoglycemia (especially elderly/renal impairment)
Blood dyscrasias (agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia)
Severe skin reactions (erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis)
emergency: Severe, prolonged hypoglycemia with coma or seizures

monitoring: Fasting and self-monitored blood glucose and HbA1c
Serum sodium (particularly if symptoms of fluid retention or with concomitant diuretics)
Complete blood count if signs of dyscrasia
Recognition of prolonged hypoglycemia, especially in the elderly
counsel: Take once daily with breakfast and do not skip meals - skipping meals can cause dangerously low blood sugar
Low blood sugar with this medicine can be severe and last a long time; learn the symptoms (sweating, shakiness, confusion) and how to treat it, and seek help if it does not resolve
Avoid alcohol - it can cause facial flushing, headache, and nausea, and worsen low blood sugar
Report drowsiness, confusion, swelling, or low energy that could indicate low sodium
Use sun protection, as your skin may become more sensitive to sunlight
pk: Blood-glucose-lowering effect within about 1 hour; full effect over hours
Peak plasma concentration approximately 2-4 hours after an oral dose
Up to 24 hours or longer from a single daily dose; effects can persist due to long half-life
Store at controlled room temperature (20-25 C) in a tightly closed container; protect from moisture
pearls: Long-acting sulfonylurea (half-life ~36 h) - hypoglycemia can be severe and prolonged; avoid in the elderly and in renal/hepatic impairment
Carries the sulfonylurea class warning of increased cardiovascular mortality (UGDP study)
Uniquely potentiates ADH and can cause SIADH/hyponatremia - monitor serum sodium
Disulfiram-like flushing reaction with alcohol - counsel patients to avoid alcohol
Largely superseded by shorter-acting sulfonylureas and other agents due to its safety profile
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember if it is still around breakfast time; if it is later in the day or close to the next day's dose, skip it and resume your usual once-daily schedule. Do not take two doses at once, as the medicine is long-acting and doubling raises the risk of prolonged low blood sugar.
overdose: Overdose causes hypoglycemia that may be severe and prolonged for days because of the long half-life. Treat mild hypoglycemia with oral carbohydrate; severe hypoglycemia (coma, seizures, neurological changes) requires intravenous glucose (e.g., 50% dextrose) followed by a continuous dextrose infusion, with close monitoring for at least 24-48 hours due to risk of recurrence. Octreotide may be used for refractory sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia. Monitor serum sodium and provide supportive care.
